﻿Waste reduction / recovery 


* Waste Heat Recovery


Waste Heat Recovery (WHR) doesn't generate new heat — it captures heat that's already being thrown away (mainly hot exhaust/flue gases leaving a boiler or furnace) and reuses it, most commonly to preheat the boiler's incoming feedwater or combustion air. This means the boiler needs to burn less fuel to reach the same steam output. It's the cheapest, lowest-risk technology in your whole database because it doesn't replace anything — it just makes the existing coal/biomass/gas boiler more efficient. 




Field
	Value
	Process
	Any boiler/furnace with hot exhaust gas — preheats feedwater or combustion air; also used for continuous blowdown recovery
	Temperature
	Recovers from waste streams typically 150–500°C+ (flue gas); high-temperature waste heat above 400°C is easiest/most valuable to capture
	Energy source
	None — it's a passive heat exchanger, no external energy input beyond a small pump/fan
	Efficiency
	Boosts overall boiler thermal efficiency by 2–5% for a basic economizer, up to 70–90% recovery efficiency of available exhaust enthalpy for a well-designed waste heat recovery boiler
	CAPEX
	Roughly ₹3.5 lakh for a basic MS economizer (small/medium industrial scale) — see rupee section below
	OPEX
	Very low — minimal moving parts, mainly periodic cleaning/descaling
	Lifetime
	15–20+ years (simple heat exchanger, low mechanical stress)
	Space
	Small — mounted directly on or near the existing boiler/exhaust stack, minimal footprint
	Constraints
	Needs an existing hot exhaust stream to recover from; corrosion risk if condensing below acid dew point; limited by flue gas temperature and flow.


	* Heat Exchanger 
A heat exchanger is a device that transfers heat from a hot fluid to a cold fluid without directly mixing them. It is commonly used to heat water, air, oil or another process fluid using waste heat, steam, hot water or another heat source. It can help MSMEs recover and reuse heat, reducing fuel and electricity consumption.
Field
	Value
	Process
	Water heating, pre-heating, drying, pasteurization, process heating/cooling, boiler feedwater heating and waste-heat recovery
	Temperature
	Typically ~50–400°C, depending on the heat source, exchanger material and design
	Energy source
	Recovered heat / steam / hot water / hot oil / exhaust gases; the exchanger itself does not generate heat
	Efficiency
	Typically ~70–95% heat-transfer effectiveness, depending on design and operating conditions
	CAPEX
	Roughly ₹1–5 lakh for small MSME systems → ₹5–25 lakh+ for medium systems, depending on heat-transfer area, material, temperature, pressure and capacity
	OPEX
	Low — mainly cleaning, inspection, pump operation and gasket/seal replacement
	Lifetime
	Typically 15–25 years, depending on material, temperature, corrosion and maintenance
	Space
	Compact to moderate; plate heat exchangers require relatively little space, while shell-and-tube systems need more space
	Constraints
	Fouling/scaling, corrosion, pressure and temperature limits, insufficient waste heat, fluid compatibility and regular cleaning requirements
	

* Condensate Recovery 
Condensate recovery is a heat-recovery method in which the hot water formed when steam loses heat and condenses back into water is collected and returned to the boiler or process. Instead of wasting this hot water, the MSME reuses its heat and treated water, which reduces fuel, water and chemical consumption.
Field
	Value
	Process
	Recovery of hot condensate from steam-using equipment such as dryers, heat exchangers, process vessels, sterilizers and steam pipelines
	Temperature
	Typically ~60–100°C, depending on steam pressure and how much heat is lost before recovery
	Energy source
	Recovered heat from condensate; no new primary energy is generated
	Efficiency
	Typically ~70–95% recovery potential, depending on condensate return rate, temperature and system design
	CAPEX
	Roughly ₹1–10 lakh for small MSME systems → ₹10–30 lakh+ for larger systems, depending on piping, pumps, tanks, condensate recovery equipment and capacity
	OPEX
	Low — mainly pump electricity, inspection, water treatment and maintenance of traps/pipes
	Lifetime
	Typically 15–25 years, depending on piping, pumps, water quality and maintenance
	Space
	Small–Moderate — requires condensate collection tank, pumps and piping
	Constraints
	Long/poorly insulated steam lines, condensate contamination, steam-trap failure, pressure differences, corrosion and insufficient condensate return
	

* Steam Recovery
Steam recovery is a method of capturing and reusing steam or the hot condensate produced after steam is used in an industrial process, instead of allowing that energy and water to be wasted.     




Field
	Value
	Process
	Recovers condensate and/or flash steam from steam-using equipment and returns it to the boiler/feedwater system. Hot condensate is collected from process equipment, while flash steam can be separated and reused for low-pressure heating.
	Temperature
	Typically recovers hot condensate at around 80–180°C, depending on the steam pressure and process. Higher-pressure condensate can produce useful flash steam when depressurized.
	Energy source
	No external energy source for basic condensate recovery; uses the existing pressure and temperature of the condensate. A small pump may be required for return.
	Efficiency
	Condensate recovery can reduce boiler fuel consumption by roughly 5–15%, depending on the percentage and temperature of condensate returned. Well-designed systems can recover a large fraction of available condensate/flash-steam energy.
	CAPEX
	Roughly ₹2–10 lakh for a small/medium industrial system, depending on condensate-return distance, pumps, flash tank, piping, insulation and controls.
	OPEX
	Low — mainly pump electricity, inspection, trap maintenance, water treatment and periodic cleaning.
	Lifetime
	Typically 10–20+ years for properly maintained piping, tanks, pumps and heat-recovery equipment.
	Space
	Small to medium — requires condensate collection tanks, pumps, piping and potentially a flash tank.
	Constraints
	Requires an existing steam distribution and condensate-return system. Pressure differences, contaminated condensate, steam-trap failure, corrosion, water hammer and long return-pipe distances can limit recovery.
